utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, we have your request and the annex setting out the materials which you seek. They are, if I may say so, a very broad and sweeping kind and would involve a great amount of material. That would be my first reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We are on the horns of a dilemma. On the one hand, we want to be specific and detailed and precise, and we have tried to be so, as is required. On the other hand, we want to be comprehensive and leave nothing out. So we have tried to bridge the horns of this dilemma by being as specifically clear as we can, given the fact that what we do want covers a two-year period. So I recognise the issue and I recognise the problem. With respect to Your Honour's observations, I think we have tried to be as specific as is possible under the situation. I don't want to repeat, unless Your Honour wants me to, the specifics of what we ask for. I can only be clearer, perhaps, or more repetitious, but I think the papers themselves are completely direct and pointed. Having heard the case for as long as Your Honours have, you certainly understand the relevance of all these documents. I don't think that's contested by anyone. I might add, unless Your Honour wants me to go through each of the 13 requests, as I understand the objection, the objection which, in the first instance, in my view, does not particularly comport with Rule 54 bis (F)(1) in that it does not identify, as far as possible, the basis on which the claim of national security interests would be prejudiced, really is an objection on two grounds: first, that they don't have certain documents and, second, that UNPROFOR would, indeed, be a proper place to proceed. Jumping ahead, as you know from the discussions you've had with your legal officer, UNPROFOR, in fact, does not object to many of the documents that we have requested. It's a question of finding them and bringing them into a timely conclusion. So unless Your Honour wants to hear more from me, I can only say that all of these documents, the milinfosums, the daily sit. reports, the battle war diaries, the communications between the units, particularly with regard to the various municipalities which form the basis for this indictment, all of the municipalities from Prozor to Stupni Do, Your Honours have seen over the course of the trial thus far that I'm afraid modern soldiering means spending half the time in the trenches and half the time at a typewriter, because they make reports and the reports are, in fact, the best evidence of what was happening on the ground from the various perspectives of the various participants on the ground. Ultimately, I am sure that Your Honours have concluded that whatever happened in the Lasva Valley, in an abstract, philosophic sense, was recorded on a daily basis from different people from different perspectives, different walks of life, different views, political, military, historical, all of whom were chronologicaling [phoen] the events on a daily basis. The Dutch did the same as the British, the Spanish, other units on the ground, the ECMM monitors, and we simply seek those documents which would be important and relevant in that regard. I might add that to the extent that some of the witnesses, some of the DutchBat witnesses who have testified, relied on their reports, you can see their significance. To the extent that they used their reports in preparing their testimony, you can see the significance. We simply want the units' work product, if you will, for the area and time in question. I don't know how many more ways to say that we all perceive similar events differently. Three people can perceive one event in three different ways. The perceptions in this case differ between the Prosecutor's perceptions and the multi-sided perceptions of the witnesses they have called to prove their perceptions. The best evidence of what was going on in the valley is contained in these contemporaneous journals, notes, infosums, intelligence works, et cetera. With that I'd just as soon stand down and hear what other objections there may be, other than the generic objection which was filed by the government of the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. von Hebel, we have your letter stating your objection, and including a note of notice of objection under Rule 54 bis. So we've had the opportunity of reading this document, but, of course, if there is anything you wish to add, please do so. MR. VON HEBEL: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me first start by saying that the Netherlands welcomes this opportunity to be heard in relation to this request, as it allows our government indeed to indicate where it is able to submit material and where reasons of national or international security interests or other considerations might create problems for our government to submit such information. It goes without saying, of course, that the Netherlands attaches great importance to fruitful --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were asked to slow down by the interpreters. MR. VON HEBEL: I'm sorry. And whenever and wherever possible, the government feels privileged and obliged to give the Tribunal any support possible to contribute to an effective implementation of the difficult task given to the Tribunal, it will provide us as much relevant information as possible in order to allow the Tribunal to establish criminal responsibility for persons who are charged before the Tribunal of serious violations of International Humanitarian Law. Before addressing specific remarks to each of the 13 documents and categories of information which the Defence for the accused has requested, the government would like to make a few observations of a more general character. And these observations relate, in the first place, to the efforts of the Defence to obtain documents and materials from the Netherlands; in the second place, the character of the co-operation between the Tribunal and the Netherlands in relation to the criteria to be applied in assessing the request of the Defence; and in the third place, the position and responsibility of Netherlands military units in the context of UNPROFOR in the area of Central Bosnia-Herzegovina. First, in relation to the efforts undertaken by Defence to obtain documents and materials from the Netherlands, we would like to make the following observations. By letter of 31 August 1999, the Defence for the accused Kordic requested information and materials through the Embassy of the Netherlands in the United States in Washington. That letter indicated that without a reaction to the request within ten days, the request would be considered to have been denied. By letter of 10 September 1999, the Netherlands ambassador in Washington, Mr. Vos, replied, and I quote: "Given the nature and sheer volume of the material involved, it will take some time to carry out your request. One important factor in this connection is that quite a lot of the requested of material consists of U.N. documents." The ambassador furthermore indicated that a further specification of the request would be needed, and that the request was passed on to the Netherlands Ministry of Defence. Since this exchange of letters, no contact has taken place between the Defence for the accused and the Dutch Ministry of Defence. The ministry has been further studying the request, but has not had the opportunity of informing the Defence of any progress in this case. The Defence, on the other side, has never taken the initiative to contact this ministry, either in order to specify the request or in order to learn about any possible progress. Although, admittedly, it would have been appropriate for the competent Dutch authorities to provide information to the Defence, it may at the same time be questioned whether the Defence for the accused, in light of Rule 54 bis, paragraph (b)(ii) has taken indeed all reasonable steps to obtain the documents or information from the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that we can follow the position, Mr. von Hebel, are you saying that if the Defence had approached the Ministry of Defence, it may be that some of the documents could have been made available? MR. VON HEBEL: I'm not sure whether the documents could have been available, but at least the ministry could have informed the Defence of the observations which we might have had in relation to documents. And as the ambassador in Washington has indicated, given the rather broad character of the request, it might have been useful in the co-operation between the ministry and the Defence for the accused, as it would have had more guidance as to the specific character of the documents that the Defence was looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the Ministry would find it helpful to have known, perhaps, in slightly more detail, what it is that the Defence really want? MR. VON HEBEL: I think that it would have assisted. Whether, in the end, and that is part of the story I would like to come back to at a later stage, it would have made much difference as to the possibility of handing over information, at least we would have had the opportunity, in direct contact with the Defence, to submit our observations and to provide, from our side, any information as to the character of the information requested, and which partly is in our possession and partly is not in our possession. But it would have helped, indeed, the further dealing with the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. MR. VON HEBEL: Coming, then, to the second general observation, the character of the co-operation between the Tribunal and the Netherlands. The Netherlands government would like to make a number of observations. In the judgement of 29 October 1997, on the request of the Republic of Croatia for review of the decision of Trial Chamber II of 18 July 1997, in the case of the Prosecutor versus Blaskic, the Appeals Chamber has indicated that, and I quote: "The plain wording of Article 29 of the Statute makes it clear that the obligation it creates is incumbent upon all member states, irrespective of whether or not they are states of the former Yugoslavia." This is in paragraph 29 of that judgement. In paragraph 30 of the same judgement, however, the Appeals Chamber continues with the observation that it does see some merit in a distinction drawn by the Prosecutor between, "states located on the territory of the former Yugoslavia" and "third states which were not directly involved in the conflict and whose role, then as now, is that of concerned bystanders." The Netherlands government would like to argue here that also in the present case a distinction could and should be drawn between the request for co-operation with one of the former Yugoslav republics and the request for co-operation with a bystander state, or a third state, such as the Netherlands. This is not so much a strict legal distinction -- Article 29 of the Statute applies, of course, equally to all member states -- but more a practical distinction. After all, the character of the documentation and information requested will, depending on the state requested, in all likelihood have a fundamentally different character. Such information stemming from one of the former Yugoslav republics -- former Yugoslav republic will often amount to important evidence for establishing individual criminal responsibility of persons accused of crimes falling under the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. Such evidence may, for example, relate to the sources or addressees of specific orders to commit such crimes, to change of command, et cetera. After all, as has in the meantime become clear from the functioning of this Tribunal, government officials from several of such Yugoslav republics have regularly been actively involved in the commission of such crimes. On the other hand, however, material requested from a third state will, in all likelihood, not contain such information. Such states have, one may assume, not been involved in the commission of crimes falling under the Tribunal's jurisdiction. They have not given orders to commit such crimes and have not formed part of any chain of command used for the commission of such crimes. It may not ever be excluded that documents from such third states may provide, in a more indirect way, information about the functioning of persons and organs active in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. It automatically follows from this difference in character of the information that the criteria used in balancing security interests of part of a state against the interests of the Tribunal, or the interests of parties involved in proceedings before the Tribunal, have to be interpreted somewhat differently. This difference in character also influences the interpretation and application of the four criteria for the issuance of binding orders, applied by the Appeals Chamber in the afore quoted October 1997 Blaskic judgement, and also in the decision of 9 September of last year, on the request of the Republic of Croatia for review of a binding order in the present case under consideration by this Trial Chamber. Finally, also the fact that the present request stems from the Defence for the accused, influences the application of the aforementioned criteria. In cases of information provided to the Prosecutor on the confidential basis, Rule 70, paragraph (B), provides adequate safeguards for preserving the confidentiality of such information. In relation to requests for information from the Defence, no such guarantees are provided for in the Rules. The fact that Defence for the accused, in its letter of 31 August 1999, has stipulated to preserve the confidentiality of information requested, does not amount to a similar obligation as rests upon the Prosecutor under the Rules and, consequently, not to a similar guarantee for the state concerned for the confidentiality of the information provided. The Netherlands government hastens to repeat here that in the end, the decision on the application and interpretation of these criteria remains entirely within the powers of the Judges of the Tribunal, and that any such decision is binding for all U.N. member states. In relation to the question of national security interests, it is the view of this government that a wider margin should be allowed to third states in invoking national security interest than to former Yugoslav republics. The interests of such third states will normally not relate to pieces of information that will assist the Tribunal in establishing criminal responsibility of persons charged with such crimes or in establishing crimes for the non-existence of such criminal responsibility. Almost by definition, such security interests of third states will not relate to the behaviour of persons charged with crimes under the Tribunal's jurisdiction. After all, the persons charged before this Tribunal do not have the nationality of the third state, have not acted on their behalf, and the acts of these persons charged have not taken place on the territory of the third state. Finally, such persons have normally not been in the custody of a third state. As there is therefore, in general, no jurisdictional relationship between the alleged perpetrator and that third state, it will in practice be rather unlikely that such a state will have relevant information that relates to the alleged behaviour of the accused. One may in principle argue here that there may be a presumption that third states will not have material relevant for establishing individual criminal responsibility of persons charged with crimes falling under the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, unless, of course, there exists specific indications to the contrary. There rests a burden on the party requesting such material to provide such contrary indications. This also means that if such a third state invokes national security interests, those interests will normally not relate to possible evidence on the criminal responsibility of the accused. The government would furthermore like to argue that the interpretation and application of the four criteria for the issuance of binding orders established in the case law of this Tribunal needs to be seen in a different light when it applies to a former Yugoslav republic, on the one hand, or a third state, on the other. The government would argue, in particular, that the interpretation and application of the second and third criteria may need further clarification. These criteria relate to the requests -- that the request should set out succinctly the reasons why such documents are deemed relevant to the trial and that the requests should not be unduly onerous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just deal with the point about relevance. That is very much a matter for the Trial Chamber, and I think it's been said in other cases that it's not a matter for the respondent governments, because only we know what the relevant issues are. Of course, the second point is one very much for governments to make submissions on, because only they will know how onerous it might be to recover documents. MR. VON HEBEL: Thank you in that respect, and that is also the reason why our observations in relation to the interpretation and application of these criteria we have combined, indeed, in light of the clear case law of the Tribunal that the question of the relevance is an issue of exclusive responsibility for the Tribunal itself. We do think, however, that if a request is directed to a third state, the requesting party is under a stronger burden to indicate the possible relevance of the material for a trial, and in order -- therefore with the result that the relevance of the material may be taken into account when balancing the production of material -- whether the production of material would, indeed, be unduly onerous for a state when requested to produce an enormous amount of documentation. In relation to this criterion, the Appeals Chamber, in the decision on the requests of Croatia for review of a binding order of 9th September 1999, emphasised that this third criterion is, by definition, a relative one. In paragraph 41 of this decision, the Appeals Chamber argued that, I quote: "It entails a striking of a balance to a need, on the one hand, for the Tribunal to have the assistance of states in the collection of evidence for the purpose of prosecuting persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law and the need, on the other hand, to ensure that the obligation upon states to assist the Tribunal in the evidence-collecting process is not unfairly burdensome." In this balancing, it is obvious that as soon as the possible relevance of information for the purpose of collection of evidence becomes more doubtful, the production of this information becomes more easily unfairly burdensome. Before providing our comments on the 13 categories of information, the government would like to further clarify the presence and role of Dutch military units in Central Bosnia-Herzegovina within the context of the UNPROFOR operation in that area. A complete overview of the Netherlands military presence in the framework of UNPROFOR is provided in an annex which we will provide in writing to the Tribunal. For purposes of the present hearing, however, it suffices to focus primarily on the organisational structure of UNPROFOR and the position of Dutch military personnel within that structure. The UNPROFOR was established by Security Council Resolution 743 of 21 March 1992. It later became known as the United Nations Peace Force, UNPF, and lasted until the North Atlantic Treaty Implementation Force, IFOR, was created in December 1995, later followed by the Stabilisation Force, SFOR. The Netherlands was one of many to participate in UNPROFOR and the UNPF, and throughout the operation a variety of Dutch units were deployed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. These units were present in various locations from the date of inception of UNPROFOR until the end of the operation. Some of these units remained in the area as part of the Netherlands' commitment to IFOR and later SFOR, and some are, in fact, still present in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. Netherlands participation in UNPROFOR and UNPF was varied and included headquarter staff personnel, signals and communications personnel, transport and logistics units, military police units, infantry units, and military observers. These units operated in a variety of tasks and from a variety of locations. In the same annex, a more detailed description of the kind of personnel, their mandates and their positions, is further elaborated. For purposes of this hearing, however, it suffices here to indicate that the presence of the Netherlands in Central Bosnia-Herzegovina consisted primarily of: one, a logistics and transportation battalion, in the period under consideration, based for most of the time in Busovaca; two, signals and communications personnel present in a different part of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Central Bosnia-Herzegovina; and, three, a small number of United Nations military observers. Of major importance for the response to the request for material by the Defence of the accused is the command and control structure of UNPROFOR, UNPF, and the U.N. military observers, UNMO. In this connection, it is important to make two distinctions. Firstly, there's a difference between administrative command and control and operational command and control. The first type of command and control refers to all matters relating to maintaining a unit, including supply of provisions, personnel rotation, salaries, wages, and the like. The second type of command and control refers to all matters relating to the actual operation of a unit, including its tasks and methods of operation, and often laid down in standard operating procedures. The functioning of a unit in a larger military operation as a whole should be taken into account here. The second distinction which must be made is that the command and control relationships for the UNMOs were different from those applicable to all other Netherlands personnel in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. The Netherlands maintained administrative control and a command and control over all Netherlands units in the former Yugoslavia, with the exception of the UNMOs, but transferred the operational command and control to the United Nations upon deployment in the theatre of operation. Regional units reported to and were controlled by regional headquarters which, in turn, in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, reported to and were controlled by Bosnia-Herzegovina command headquarters in Sarajevo. Bosnia-Herzegovina command, in turn, reported to and was controlled by the UNPROFOR headquarters and the UNPROFOR force commander in Zagreb. UNPROFOR headquarters and UNPROFOR force commanders finally reported to and were controlled by the United Nations Department of Peacekeeping Operations. In other words, the chain of command for UNPROFOR and the UNPF was wholly a United Nations chain of command. National headquarters did not participate in any way or at any point in the UNPROFOR or UNPF chain of command. In the standard operating procedure, for example, such national headquarters are explicitly not included in the distribution lists of operational command and control information. In addition to administrative command and control, the Netherlands, of course, maintains so-called full command of Netherlands units deployed in UNPROFOR and UNPF. This term of art, "full command," however, refers to the authority vested in the national government to decide whether or not to prolong participation of any or all of its units in any given operation. It does not include, and in fact the United Nations guidelines for peacekeepers expressly prohibits, direct operational control over the units, giving operational instructions to the units, or receiving operational information from the units. Finally, while units and contingents operate as national units under United Nations command and control, UNMOs, on the other hand, operate on an individual basis under the United Nations command and control. Such personnel is, in essence, provided, quote/unquote, "on loan to the United Nations" and enters into a contractual relationship with the United Nations which seems similar to direct employment with the United Nations. The command and control over such personnel is therefore carried out even more fully by the United Nations than in the case of, quote/unquote, "regular units and contingents." The command and control structure is further elaborated in the standard operating procedures issued by the U.N. peacekeeping operations office in New York. These procedures are, in itself, confidential United Nations material, but the government is, however, willing, if the Trial Chamber should so wish, to provide, on a confidential basis, to the Trial Chamber, copies of the relevance parts of these procedures. Mr. President, the government would now like to turn to the 13 categories of documents and information which have been identified by the Defence and which are requested from the Netherlands government. The first material requested by the Defence relates to the so-called battalion war diary for units of the Dutch army. Although this government is aware of the fact that a number of states have a practice of keeping such diaries, it must inform the Tribunal, though, that such diaries have not been kept by any of the Dutch army units in Central Bosnia-Herzegovina in the material period. No such diaries can therefore be produced. The second category of material requested relate to the so-called daily situation reports or equivalent records. Such reports were made by the various regional military units in the area and, according to the standard operation procedure, sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina command headquarters in Sarajevo and subsequently to UNPROFOR headquarters. These reports related to the operational command and control of UNPROFOR and were meant for exclusive use by UNPROFOR. According to the distribution lists for these reports as laid down in the standard operating procedure, national army headquarters were not provided with copies of such reports. The Netherlands government therefore has to inform the Tribunal that no such reports are available within the Dutch administration and no such reports can therefore be produced. But even if the Netherlands government would have such information, it would still not be in a position to provide copies of such reports, as these are normally and mostly U.N.-classified materials. Whether the material might be declassified or provided to a party to a procedure before the Tribunal is a decision which rests entirely with the United Nations. It would seriously undermine the organisation of peacekeeping operations, past, present and future, by the United Nations if U.N. member states and contributing countries would individually decide about a declassification or publication of such information. It is for this particular reason, Mr. President, that the Netherlands government, by letter of 10 January 2000, felt obliged to send you a notice of objection pursuant to Rule 54 bis (F) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal. As indicated in that letter, the government file does not notice not so much for national security interests of the Netherlands stricti sensu but for the security interests of the United Nations in relation to the smooth and safe functioning of all peacekeeping operations. The United Nations, its member states, and the particular states contributing to peacekeeping operations, must be able to rely on procedures and agreements made in advance. Making public information which was gathered in a confidential way and meant to remain confidential, unless the United Nations, of course, itself would decide otherwise, would undermine the confidence in such procedures and agreements. This would obviously also have an influence on present and future peacekeeping operations. As far as such classified material has, in the meantime, been declassified by the United Nations itself or been used for reports of the United Nations organisation -- or been used for reports of the United Nations organisation not of a classified character, such material is obviously easily accessible to every interested person. The Netherlands government would like to stress here that these observations apply mutatis mutandis to most of the other categories of material requested by the Defence. In order to avoid repetition and save time, this will be briefly indicated wherever this is the case, in the understanding that the arguments just presented will equally apply to such categories of material as well. Finally, in relation to this second category of material requested, the government would like to observe that the request of information, as such, is formulated in rather general terms. A further specification, at least in time, of the relevant reports requested would have been appropriate. In light, for example, of the indictments of the two accused in this case, the Netherlands government fails to see why material unrelated grationi [phoen] de temporis to the indicted offences, that is to say, after March 1994, might be relevant for the Defence of the accused. Also, this argument applies to most of the other information requested by the Defence for the accused. The Defence furthermore does not provide any reasons why this request number 2 is formulated in such broad terms and why the request apparently could not be formulated more precisely, and furthermore does not provide sufficient information on the question why such documents are deemed relevant to the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's very much a matter for us. We've heard much evidence about documents of various sorts, and we really are in the best position to judge that. If you could go on, Mr. von Hebel, to the other matters. If the same argument applies as under paragraph 2, perhaps you could just briefly make that point. MR. VON HEBEL: Sure. The third category of material relates to the military information summaries, or so-called milinfosums, and equivalent records. The argument as to the security interests involved relating to the material covered by number 2 applies mutatis mutandis to this category of material. This material is also classified United Nations material, and according to the standard operating procedures, the distribution of milinfosums is identical to those of daily situation reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the position is exactly the same. MR. VON HEBEL: It's exactly the same, indeed. Also the request for this third category of material lacks specificity. The comments, on the wide scope, in substance and time period, as I indicated a moment ago, apply equally over here. The fourth category of material requested by the Defence for the accused relates to, I quote, "any written communication, record or document," prepared by Dutch army or intelligence personnel and relating to civil and military command structures of several Croatian entities. As to the access to this category of information, I would like to refer back to our observations in relation to the material requested under number 2. Furthermore, the Netherlands government likes to observe also that this category of material is formulated in even broader terms than the preceding two categories. In light of the case law of the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal of 9 September 1999, we just wonder whether this request meets the requirement of specificity, clearly prohibiting the use of broad categories. It therefore lies with the Defence to further clarify the scope of this request or to justify this broad scope of the request. In addition, as this request number 4 not only refers to Dutch army personnel, but also to Dutch intelligence personnel, government would like to stress here that in the context of UNPROFOR, the military personnel deployed in Central Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the period covered by the request, consisted largely of a transportation battalion and a signals battalion. It does not belong to the mandate of such personnel to undertake intelligence activities. The fifth category of information relates to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could I make sure I've got the submission on the 4th. Is this in the same category as 2 and 3, or may there be documents available there, although you make other points about it? MR. VON HEBEL: It does indeed cover the same categories of information as under 2 and 3, as they relate exclusively to the operational command and control structure of UNPROFOR, Mr. President. The fifth category of information relates, as I indicated, to any written communication submitted by or on behalf of units of the Dutch army to Dutch army headquarters for certain periods of time indicated in the request and relating to offence in certain municipalities. The Netherlands government first refers back to previous comments as regards the confidential character of the -- of most of the information covered by this category. But here again the request, and in particular the reference to "any written communication" seems again to be broad and lacking specific specificity. The request by the Defence of the accused also lacks any reasoning for the broad scope of the request. In relation to the specific locations mentioned in the request, the government would like to observe that Netherlands units or personnel were not necessarily present in or near the locations listed during the time periods indicated. The transportation battalion and the signals battalion were present in or operating in the vicinity of Vitez, Travnik, Novi Travnik and Busovaca in the period indicated, and may have been present near Gornji Vakuf and Bugogno in the period indicated as well. To indicate with any degree of certainty whether Netherlands units were present in or near the other locations indicated during the time period would require analysis of every transportation and communication orders given and carried out by United Nations during the deployment of the Netherlands units in UNPROFOR. Also, this kind of information, however, forms part of the operational command and control documents of UNPROFOR. The kind of material requested in the list of materials to be produced under number 6 are by far the most generally and broadly formulated of all categories. It relates to, and I quote, "any contemporaneous official or unofficial diary, journal, or other written record of daily activities and events maintained by Dutch army or intelligence personnel deployed in Central Bosnia-Herzegovina from that date of deployment until 31 December 1994." The material, as can be interpreted, sought here basically relates to any piece of paper prepared by any person who has served in one of the military units present in Bosnia-Herzegovina over a period of more than two years. My government in this case fails to see how this request can meet the criteria of specificity. In addition, it is impossible for the government to try to get hold of any material of an unofficial character. In our view, a government can only be requested to produce official information which has been produced or received in the course of the exercise of its functions. Any unofficial material, the existence of which might not even be known to a government, can, in all reasonableness, not be expected to be produced. As the official documentation is concerned, here to a large extent the same argumentation should be followed as in relation to the request under number 2. In relation to the intelligence personnel, I would like also, for reasons of time saving, to refer back to our observations under number 4. In one respect, however, the information sought here differs from all previous categories. Given the very broad character in which this request is formulated, this request may also relate to information of a purely housekeeping character, to put it that way. That means information relating to the administrative command and control over the military units deployed in the area. The exchange of such information was not governed by UNPROFOR regulations. UNPROFOR regulations and such exchanges took place between military units in the area of deployment and national headquarters. At this moment, however, the request is, in the view of this government, insufficiently specified. The request, furthermore, clearly lacks succinct reasoning as to the relevance of such information and to the balancing of the relevance of the information in relation to the burden upon our government to produce such documentation. In our view, such an approach of merely requesting such broad categories of information seems to be incompatible with the criteria set out by this Tribunal. In our view, therefore, this information should be considered as to be unduly onerous in relation to the exigencies of the trial. The Netherlands government would furthermore not exclude also, in light of the purely administrative character of such material, that such exchanges of information have never been duly registered and put in archives. Even if such information was registered and archived at the time, and again here, in light of the character of the information, it may very well be that such information has in the meantime been destroyed. The Netherlands government has, however, not yet been able to sufficiently identify and search for such documentation; also in light of the broadness of the request. Upon request, of course, of the Trial Chamber, the government would be most willing to try to further identify and search for such information and to report back on the possible availability of such documentation. In relation to the documentation requested under numbers 7 and 8, documentation relating to photographs or videotape recordings, we would refer back again to our observations in relation to number 2. The photo or video material fall within the category of the operational command and control of UNPROFOR at that time. According to the standard operation procedures, even the taking of pictures by persons not explicitly authorised to do so are strictly prohibited, and such -- if the taking of such material was taken, could be punished by the competent authorities within UNPROFOR. Furthermore, in relation to the issue of Dutch intelligence units, I would like to refer back to our observations in relation to request number 4 and 6. The material requested under number 9 relate to any sort of records of the next military working group. This working group was, according to the standard operation procedures, a high-level group for military negotiations with the warring factions. Obviously, this kind of information would fall within the operational command and control of UNPROFOR, and therefore we would like to refer back to our observations and objections under number 2. The information requested under number 10, radio transmission logs of Dutch army and intelligence units, is again a category formulated in a rather broad way. It is furthermore unclear what the Defence means exactly when referring to radio transmission logs. These can be interpreted either referring to the methods of communication between the units in Central Bosnia-Herzegovina and Dutch army headquarters, or to the content of such communications. Since the request relates to communications with Dutch army headquarters, they cannot relate to operational information, as such information was, as indicated earlier, strictly exchanged within UNPROFOR channels. By definition, such radio logs would relate to logistical administrative matters. Given again the purely housekeeping character of the material, the Netherlands authorities have never kept any records of the use of such methods of communication; that is to say, when, where, and between whom matters of communication were used. Furthermore, no records have ever been made of the content of such communication. As to the question of intelligence units, I obviously refer back to previous observations and requests, number 4 inter alia. Finally, Mr. President, the materials requested under categories 11 and 12, the disposition of warring forces maps, or any situation maps, and category 13, the orders of battle and related material. Again the Netherlands government has to stress that such material relates to the operational command and control of UNPROFOR, and therefore refers back to our observations in relation to request number 2. May I come to a conclusion, Mr. President. As stated at the beginning of this intervention, our government welcomes very much the opportunity to be heard on the request by the Defence. The government wants to stress again that it attaches great importance to a fruitful cooperation, and it feels obliged and honoured if it can provide in any reasonable and meaningful way any sort of assistance in the production of material that may contribute to a fair trial for persons prosecuted for responsibility of serious violations of International Humanitarian Law. The Netherlands government was, however, forced here to file objections to the requests, for both pragmatic and principled reasons. The pragmatic reason is that most material, being material relating to the operational command and control of UNPROFOR, is not available to the Netherlands authorities. The principled reason, in addition, is that even if such material would have been available, such material touches upon security interests of the United Nations. And again I would like to reiterate here that the decisions about the possible publication of such material rests entirely within the United Nations. In the analysis of all 13 categories of material requested, only in two instances material might have been involved that does not touch upon the operational command and control of UNPROFOR. In those two situations the requests under number 6 and 10 to material relates to purely administrative, logistical information. Under number 10, however, as explained, these radio logs, whether interpreted in a technical or in a substantial way, were not considered of sufficient importance as to make any records of such logs. Under number 6, apart from the question that the request lacks sufficient specificity, the question should first be answered whether, in light of the criteria, these categories of documentation are of any relevance, and of such relevance as to balance the interests of the state, not to be confronted with unduly onerous requests for the production of information. In this respect, Mr. President, the Netherlands government would like briefly to refer back to its general observations in this statement, according to which, certainly in practice, in balancing these interests, a distinction should be made between requests directed to any of the former Yugoslav republics and requests directed to any third state, such as in this case the Netherlands. Finally, Mr. President, the Netherlands government would like to express its full confidence in the Trial Chamber, that if the Chamber would, in light of all observations made, decide to issue an order to the Netherlands government for the production of certain material, sufficient time would be given for compliance with such an order. Thank you for your attention, and I apologise for the length of my intervention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no need to apologise. We are grateful for your assistance in the matter, Mr. von Hebel. Can I deal with two matters. The first I should have dealt with at the outset, and that is that there are only two of us, Judge Robinson being absent for urgent personal reasons, as I hope you were told. What we propose, unless there is any objection, is that we hear your arguments, as we've done. We shall not make any decisions upon them, because we could only do that as a full Trial Chamber. Judge Robinson will, of course, have the transcripts before him and will join in the decision. But, clearly, it is more convenient, since this matter was listed, to hear the arguments today. And unless there is any objection, that is what we propose to do. I take it there is no objection? Could I just, so that I have in mind, really, what you are saying. Effectively, it's this: that you have none of the material available except for diaries which may be available, but for the moment you haven't yet identified that. If there were any orders relating to the specific documents, you would wish or may wish in due course to provide the detail which will be necessary to sustain a national security objection? Would that summarise your position fairly? MR. VON HEBEL: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. I think that in relation to this material which might be -- it relates to request number 6 -- if the Court would provide an order to produce such documents, given the non-operational character of this information, at the moment I would think that such information under this category, as long as it does not relate to operational command and control structures of UNPROFOR, would not fall under any objections as to national security. My observation was primarily aimed at indicating that these are rather of a housekeeping character, and I don't see much national security interests --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the Defence were to approach you with a more specific request, you could deal with that? MR. VON HEBEL: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. von Hebel, I believe there is also the fact, to which Judge May has just said, that there are certain documents which you might have on the list, but which, in your opinion, are part of the UNPROFOR, which is a subsidiary body of the United Nations, so that even if you had them, you could not supply them, because they fall under the jurisdiction, because they make part of the security of the United Nations and, therefore, any member state may not really dispose of them freely, because they are part of the United Nations documentation? Did I understand you well? MR. VON HEBEL: Well, thank you for this question. Yes, indeed. Of course it is very difficult in general if -- as long as we do not know exactly how the order or the request should look like, and to give a statement as to national security. But as long as such information would relate to non-operational aspects of our Dutch participation in UNPROFOR, at the moment I do not think that there would be any problems of national security. But here again, in the understanding that they would primarily be of housekeeping character. If it would be more of a general nature relating to our operations of UNPROFOR, of course then we might have a problem. But as long as that is not the case, I do, at the moment, at least, not see any serious problems. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I suppose I should observe that everything in life is a matter of perspective. Imagine if the documents that we seek, in one form or another, if the Dutch conclusion that Dario Kordic had minimal, if any, role whatsoever to do with the events in Lasva Valley. Imagine if they set out with specificity and detail the relationship between the HVO, the HDZ, et cetera, in ways totally different from that which has been presented thus far. Those are the kinds of exculpatory information that we would be looking for. The Prosecution has told us in this case that because of the volumes of information, the massive quantities of information that they have, they have not been able to make a complete search for exculpatory information, or evidence materially favourable to the accused. The perspective that the government of the Netherlands brings to this case is that, from their perspective, we should be asking the provinces of the former Yugoslavia for information. In fact, the most neutral and detached, if you will, observers of the theatre were the foreign observers in that theatre, and their evidence has been the primary bulk of the Prosecution's case. And their evidence, the evidence of the UNPROFOR forces, the British forces, has always been backed up by reports, milinfosums, writings and diaries. And those writings and diaries have contained materially favourable or exculpatory information on a regular and continuing basis. So that the distinction that the Netherlands makes of a third party state versus a participant, while interesting, and used as a subway to start a standard that we would have to mount, doesn't take us, as a practical matter, where we want to go, and where the Court should be going. The United Nations organised an organisation, organised this Court, organised what went on in Yugoslavia by way of the UNPROFOR forces, and various member states joined. And there are documents that are relevant and important to this procedure. If I may be specific going through the 13 categories, and I'll be very brief. What they don't have, they don't have, so I'll skip to paragraph 3. The military information sums. or equivalent records are terribly important. I've said that over and over again. They are the best contemporaneous journal of what happened. And the Dutch officers who have testified thus far have relied upon them in their testimony. We seek not just the ones that the Prosecution has shown us, but the others that exist as well. As to category -- as to request number 4, documentation between and communications prepared by the Dutch army or intelligence personnel deployed in Central Bosnia, describing the command structure of the HVO, HZ-HB, HR-HB. That's the nub of this case. There is massive confusion on the part of the Prosecution as to what these structures are, who were in them, at what period of time, and their relationship to each other. Again, if this is contained originally in the Dutch information and now submitted to the United Nations, so be it. As to paragraph 5, we list the various towns in the indictment, we list the various periods. And, parenthetically, while I am thinking about periods, of course we did ask beyond March of 1994. Your Honour knows there's been evidence beyond March of 1994, where we've taken the evidence and testimony about events of 1995. And hence we have not limited ourselves to the period in the indictment, although I would have liked to, because it was my objection that was overruled by Your Honour. But as to the specific towns, Your Honour, I'm sure, will remember -- Your Honours will remember, Prozor was the site of fighting between the ABiH and HVO in November of '92. Gornji Vakuf was subject to numerous Muslim attacks, starting in June of '92. Bugogno, subjected to Muslim attacks, and fell in July of '93. Vitez, obvious. Fojnica --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, we are being asked, could you slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I hope the record will reflect I am doing better than when I was at full hyper speed, however. Fojnica was the site of a Muslim offensive against the HVO on 2 July 1993. And after this attack, 70 per cent of the villages in that municipality were destroyed. Travnik was subject to Muslim attacks and fell in June of 1993. Novi Travnik, included in the amended indictment, the relevance is obvious. Zepce, subject to Muslim attacks in June of '93 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, we know all of this. The issue is: Were any Dutch personnel there? That was the point which Mr. von Hebel made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And of course we don't know unless we ask. And if the answer is no, so be it, but let's have a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stein, you are presenting your list, and you say all the documents, any written communication by any and so on, everything, everything. And, you see, a government during a period of so many years, of course, collects everything. But you say here official and non-official, formal and informal, everything that a government has collected over a number of years. That is all the documents relevant for this or that question and concerning your client. This is your approach? You turn to a representative of a country and you say, "We want it all." That is, they have to go to their archives for such-and-such period of time and they give it to you. No mention, of course, of the cost of all of that; that is, the time that goes into it and the cost. And I must say this is a rather peculiar request, when one says "everything," because within that there may be things which concern your client and there may be things that do not concern your client. But you say all the documents which have a bearing on such-and-such a case or on something else, or on such-and-such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, again that's the horns of the dilemma we are on. We want to be inclusive. We want not to be so defined as to say, "Well, you didn't ask precisely for a specific piece of paper. Your category wasn't quite clear and therefore this doesn't fall within it." We don't want that kind of situation. So we on the horns of a dilemma. We would be perfectly happy to limit this request in paragraph 5 and 6 to references to Mr. Kordic specifically or to the villages that are subject to the amended indictment. But you understand, I hope again, as a matter of perspective, that when we draft these things, we do it with an eye to getting what we seek and that which we perceive there is in the government's hands, yet, on the other hand, allowing ourselves flexibility, if there are a whole category of things, documents, requests, that cover the concept, but we haven't named specifically. And so we can't be accused of, "You didn't ask for it. We are not turning it over."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At the same time -- and this is really a glorified fishing expedition, isn't it? You are just going to ask for everything the government has which might help. You don't know what these documents are, in the sense of being able to identify them. You would say you are not in a position to do it, of course. But really what you want is to troll through the documents in the hope that something will turn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: There was a time I might have agreed with you. But having read the papers that we have read thus far, at this point in the case we don't want another sea of paper. We would like to be as specific as we can. So while I understand logically you are correct, I am telling you, practically, we want to be -- try to be as narrow as we can. On the other hand, what I foresee is if you grant the request and the parties work together to honour, to try to produce the request, in particular with UNPROFOR, as a practical matter, when we look at the indexes, we see how things are kept, we'll separate wheat from chaff. We'll say this: It's been a rare milinfosum, it's been a rare British document, from any of the British Battalions that we've looked at, that hasn't had something in it that was helpful to one of our multiple issues and our multiple defences; whether it be de facto, de jure, whether it be military necessity, they all have great interest to our case. So, logically, yes, some of these things look like classic discovery requests in a civil case, and we are not trying to proceed that way. When we looked at the specific kinds of documents that we've had thus far given to us by the Prosecution, the Prosecution, having been given the documents by the various member states armed forces, we have always found something useful, that categories popped up, and you can see where we are coming from. Photographs and video recordings, I believe, are obvious on their face. I won't burden them any more. As to the mixed military working group, that would be paragraph 9, we do have the minutes of those meetings, quite frankly, and we've made much use of them, so the consequence of that is not a particularly high priority. The radio logs are submissions. I accept the representative of the Netherlands' categorisations. I would suggest they could be limited to references to Kordic or the villages that are the subject of the amended indictment. The maps in 11, 12, and 13, situation maps, are all, of course, particularly important to where the forces were on the ground at any given period of time in terms of self-defence and the defence of the various villages. The last thing I will say, because I know we're a tad short on time, is relative to efforts made before filing. Again, it's a perception problem. We would love to spend time meeting, talking, resolving these things without bringing this to the Court's attention. Thus far, we've been able to do that with the government of Great Britain. However, in the press of trial, as we're marching on, you just have to file at some point in time. The discussion started, letter writings in August, and finally by October, as we were nearing the recess, it was time to file and perhaps withdraw. If there had been some substantive discussions afterwards, perhaps these could have been resolved or they could have been resolved now. But we are now at the close of the Prosecution's case. We're going to ask for an order allowing the member states and UNPROFOR to have 60 days to respond. You know our schedule. So the press of events has its own momentum, its own steam and its own life, and sometimes you just have to litigate as opposed to talk, and so we filed. We're still more than willing to work any differences in interpretation out, but at least we need some obvious lever, with the Government of the Netherlands and the other parties present today, to begin the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider these matters, and we will issue our order in due course. Meanwhile, we'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.
